opus-5.5.text:
I think the surprise says more about where people were looking than about DeepSeek itself. From our side at vLLM, they didn't come out of nowhere. Before the big moment there was a steady stream of work: DeepSeek V2 with Multi-head Latent Attention, the MoE architecture with many fine-grained experts, and a lot of very careful engineering. When V2 came out, supporting MLA properly was real work for us, because it changes how the KV cache is laid out and how attention kernels have to be written. So the people who had to implement these models already knew this team was doing serious, original things.

What surprised the broader public, I think, was two things together. One was the cost story, the idea that you could train a frontier-level model with a fraction of the compute people assumed you needed. The other was that it was fully open, with weights and quite detailed technical reports, so anyone could verify it and run it. Usually you get one or the other: a strong closed model, or an open model a generation behind. DeepSeek V3 and then R1 gave both at once, and R1 showed reasoning ability that people had associated only with the top closed labs.

For the inference community it was a kind of stress test. These models are huge, hundreds of billions of parameters with sparse activation, so you can't just put them on one GPU and call it done. You need expert parallelism, good MLA kernels, FP8 support, multi-token prediction for speculative decoding, and eventually prefill-decode disaggregation. DeepSeek also open-sourced a lot of their infrastructure, things like FlashMLA, DeepEP, and DeepGEMM, during their open source week. That made a big difference, because we could learn from how they actually serve the model at scale and bring those ideas into an open, general-purpose engine.

So my view is that the surprise was partly a perception gap. Many people believed that the best work would only come from a few well-funded labs in the US, and that open source would always trail behind. DeepSeek showed that a focused team with strong engineering culture, and a willingness to go deep on efficiency at every layer, from model architecture down to communication kernels, can change the frontier. For people building open infrastructure like vLLM, that was very encouraging. It showed that the open ecosystem isn't just a follower. It can be where the important ideas come from.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes surprise to the broader public’s perception of DeepSeek’s cost, openness, and capabilities. It says the vLLM team already saw DeepSeek doing serious work; it does not identify DeepSeek’s unexpectedly large influence as the team’s source of surprise.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes DeepSeek as doing serious, original work known to people implementing its models. It does not characterize DeepSeek’s standing in the 2024 vLLM community as an ordinary model vendor.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, from where I sat, the surprise felt a bit strange, because for people working on open-source inference infrastructure, DeepSeek wasn't a sudden appearance at all.

I got to know them through vLLM. When they released DeepSeek-V2 in 2024, with the MLA attention design and a fairly large MoE architecture, they needed the open-source inference stack to actually support it well. So their engineers came to the vLLM community, opened issues, submitted pull requests, and discussed with us how to make the model run efficiently. That's how the collaboration started. What struck me then was how serious they were. They weren't just throwing a checkpoint over the wall and saying "good luck." They understood inference deeply, they understood the GPU memory hierarchy, and they cared about whether ordinary users could actually run their model. That's not common.

So when R1 came out in January 2025 and the whole world reacted as if a company had appeared out of nowhere, my feeling was: this is a group that has been doing very solid, very grounded engineering for a long time. V2, V3, the technical reports, the way they wrote about training costs and infrastructure details — all of that was public. If you were reading the papers and watching the repositories, the trajectory was visible.

I think the surprise came from a mismatch in attention. A lot of the public discussion about AI was centered on Silicon Valley, on how many GPUs you had, on scaling narratives. DeepSeek was operating in a different context, with export restrictions, with fewer chips, and that pushed them to squeeze much more out of every piece of hardware. That's exactly the kind of work the inference community cares about, so to us it looked like excellent engineering rather than magic. To people who were only tracking the frontier labs, it looked like a shock.

The other piece is openness. They released weights, they released detailed reports, and they engaged with open-source projects like vLLM as genuine collaborators. That lowered the barrier for everyone to try the model, which is partly why the reaction was so fast and so broad. If you can download the model and run it the same week, the conversation changes very quickly.

So I'd say the "surprise" was really a surprise about where good work can come from, not about whether the work itself was sudden. From inside the open-source community, it felt more like a steady accumulation finally becoming visible.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the surprise to DeepSeek’s sudden visibility to the wider public, not to the unexpectedly large scale of its influence surprising Kaichao You’s team.

r002.rationale: The response portrays DeepSeek as a serious engineering collaborator that contributed to vLLM, rather than as an ordinary model vendor.

astra-6.text:
I think the surprise depends on where you were watching from. For many people, DeepSeek seemed to appear suddenly. But when you work on inference infrastructure like vLLM, you pay attention to models earlier, because you need to understand their architectures and how to support them efficiently. From that perspective, it felt less like something coming out of nowhere.

That said, collaborating on model support doesn’t mean you know everything about a team’s training process or what its next release will achieve. There’s a big difference between seeing interesting technical work and knowing how much impact it will have.

So I’d separate the technical progress from the public reaction. You can see a team making progress gradually, and then one release brings all of that work to a much wider audience. To that audience, it feels sudden.

r001.rationale: The response says a release brought DeepSeek’s work to a wider audience, but it does not identify the unexpectedly large scale of its influence as the source of surprise for You’s team.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe DeepSeek’s standing in the 2024 vLLM community or characterize it as an ordinary model vendor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the surprise depends on how closely you were following DeepSeek beforehand. Through our collaboration on vLLM, I already knew they had a very strong technical team. So when their models attracted widespread attention, I was less surprised by their capabilities than by how suddenly everyone outside that circle noticed them.

There’s also a difference between building a good model and making it practical to use. Our collaboration gave me a view into the engineering work around running those models efficiently. From that perspective, their rise felt less like something appearing out of nowhere and more like sustained technical work finally becoming visible.

r001.rationale: The response says he was surprised by how suddenly people outside the technical circle noticed DeepSeek, but does not clearly identify the unexpectedly large scale of its influence as the source of surprise.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize DeepSeek’s standing in the vLLM community in 2024 as that of an ordinary model vendor.
